column3: It repeats the plea against those who led others astray, for doubled punishment in the Fire.
It grounds punishment in what hands sent ahead and denies injustice, supporting the focus's accountability claim.
Its increase in disbelief supplies a related pattern of accumulating culpability, without the focus's leader-follower scene.
The immediately preceding reply blames the speakers for having brought this fate upon the group.
It explicitly identifies this sequence as the dispute of the people of the Fire.
Repeated disbelief and its increase show escalating culpability, but do not address responsibility for others.
The shared address to the Lord and speech vocabulary do not clarify the punishment dispute.
The command to taste punishment reinforces the retributive setting, but lacks the doubled-punishment claim.
Reference to the Lord's book does not illuminate the focus's dispute over misguidance and punishment.
Those shown the Fire acknowledge its truth before being told to taste punishment for disbelief.
Hell is filled with Iblis and all who follow him, directly linking a leader and followers in one outcome.
It names Iblis as an enemy whose following displaces obedience to the Lord, supplying the source of misguidance.
Jinn and humans recount mutual influence before their shared final abode is declared to be the Fire.
It names Hell as the evil resting place within the same surah's punishment sequence.
Revelation increases some people only in aversion, a related negative escalation rather than doubled punishment.
The question over who committed an act has no material connection to leading others into the Fire.
It states that punishment is for what hands sent ahead and that Allah is not unjust to servants.
The Lordship formula alone does not clarify the focus's punitive accountability.
The prayer to be protected from the punishment of the Fire supplies a direct but non-disputational counterpart.
Following desire misleads from Allah's path and brings severe punishment, explaining the gravity of misleading others.
The statement that seeker and sought are weak is unrelated to the focus's doubled punishment.
Its repentance and plea for mercy do not develop the Fire dispute or responsibility for guidance.
Another group enters the Fire with the speakers, extending the same hostile exchange and shared punishment scene.
The question of who is Lord does not bear on the focus's request for punishment.
It explicitly joins increase with punishment: there will be no increase except in torment.
Recorded hostile speech and wrongdoing receive the command to taste burning punishment, supporting retributive speech-accountability.
Human ingratitude toward the Lord is too general to clarify the focus's accusation against misleaders.
Those who disbelieve and hinder Allah's path receive punishment added upon punishment for their corruption.
The certainty of punishment after denying messengers supplies the surah's broad retributive background.
Its increase of goodness rewards a good deed, offering only a formal contrast to increased punishment.
Weak offspring and upright speech do not bear on doubled punishment or misguidance.
It continues the same surah's description of what the condemned must taste in Hell.
A measured gift from the Lord is only a broad contrast to the focus's punitive measure.
Human weakness in battle is unrelated to the focus's punishment and leadership claim.
It confronts those who hastened the punishment once it has actually come upon them.
Revelation increases many only in rebellion and disbelief, a related worsening response to guidance.
The sequence of bodily weakness and strength does not clarify moral culpability or punishment.
It declares the transgressors' evil final return within the same punishment passage.
The confession of the Lord of Moses and Aaron is unrelated to the focus's dispute.
The weak followers confront the arrogant leaders, who admit they cannot avert Allah's punishment from them.
Wrongdoers are told to taste enduring punishment and that they are repaid only for their earnings.
The command to glorify the Lord does not develop the focus's accountability or Fire imagery.
It contrasts divine mercy with painful punishment prepared for wrongdoers, supporting the judgment setting.
Its catalogue of earlier deniers supplies the surah's historical warning context for the present punishment scene.
The statement of faith in the Lord of Moses and Aaron has no material link to the focus.
A person is informed of what was sent ahead and left behind, supporting retrospective accountability.
Allah's unchangeable judgment and denial of injustice to servants frame punishment as just, not arbitrary.
A calamity is explicitly tied to what hands sent ahead, and the anticipated response invokes the Lord.
The phrase foot of truth before the Lord does not clarify the focus's punitive use of bringing forward.
The creation and prostration command does not illuminate the Fire dispute.
The Lordship of the heavens and earth does not add to the focus's accountability theme.
Repeated presentation increases some people only in aversion, showing a related negative increase in response to guidance.
The pouring of scalding punishment supplies concrete torment imagery without the leader-follower accusation.
The desire for further worldly increase does not clarify increased punishment.
Hindering from Allah's path brings an experienced evil consequence and a great punishment.
Job's suffering called punishment is a distant lexical parallel, not the retribution of the Fire scene.
The prayer for endurance and firm feet is unrelated to the focus's punishment request.
It names guardians of the Fire and shows divergent responses to its warning, but not blame between groups.
The ironic command to taste punishment develops the same torment motif.
Return to the Lord is not a substantive link to the focus's doubled punishment.
It contrasts increased favor for believers with painful punishment for the arrogant, but lacks the focus's causal relation.
Job's healing scene does not clarify the punishment dispute.
Divine might and forgiveness supply a broad authority frame, without a direct connection to the accusation.
The deniers demand their allotment before the Day of Account, extending the surah's judgment language.
Pharaoh leads his people on the Day of Resurrection and brings them to the Fire.
Their inner disease is increased and accompanied by painful punishment for persistent lying.
Those in the Fire ask its keepers to seek one day's relief from punishment, closely matching the setting and appeal.
The next verse continues the same speakers' argument within the Fire, though it shifts to absent men.
Increase from grace for believers contrasts with severe punishment for disbelievers, without the focus's doubled retribution.
The servants pray for the punishment of Hell to be turned away, a direct devotional counterpart.
Allah's multiplying of a good loan provides a formal positive counterpart to the focus's doubled punishment.
Return to the Lord alone does not clarify the dispute over those who misled others.
A companion denies causing transgression and assigns blame to the other's prior error, closely paralleling contested responsibility.
Job's oath-related instruction does not bear on the Fire scene.
Fear of standing before the Lord offers a broad anticipatory counterpart to post-judgment punishment.
Believers ask the Lord to protect them from the punishment of the Fire.
It identifies the relevant class as deniers who are astray, supplying the condemned identity behind the punishment scene.
An increase in a camel-load of provisions is unrelated to the focus's increase in punishment.
The prayer for protection from the punishment of the Fire directly echoes the focus's address and destination.
The return of the horses has no material connection to the focus.
The reversal of oppression into leadership is only a distant contrast to destructive leadership.
The plea not to become a trial for wrongdoers does not develop the Fire dispute.
Solomon's request for forgiveness and kingdom is unrelated to doubled punishment.
Being veiled from the Lord on the Day supplies a broad judgment consequence without the focus's relational blame.
Those facing the people of the Fire ask the Lord not to place them with wrongdoers.
The announcement of human creation does not clarify the focus's punishment claim.
Abraham's submission to the Lord has no material link to the focus.
Disbelievers ask to see those who led them astray among jinn and humans so they may abase them.
Iblis's request for respite establishes his dependence on divine authority, but not the focus's punishment dispute.
The fire-destroyed garden and weak descendants are not a substantive parallel to punishment in Hell.
Assigned companions beautify wrongdoing for people until the judgment against prior jinn and human communities becomes due.
Increase in guidance for the guided is a formal positive contrast to the focus's punitive increase.
Its abasement and wrath are tied to repeated disobedience, but the request for food is otherwise unrelated.
Pharaoh's domination divides and weakens a people, supplying a concrete pattern of destructive leadership.
Its dispute about control and hidden thoughts does not clarify the focus's request for punishment.
Shared Lordship and worship do not address the focus's Fire dispute.
It locates an affliction in the people's own selves, supporting personal responsibility for consequences.
The Lord of the two eastings and westings has no material link to the focus.
Creation of pairs and transport does not clarify the focus's accountability theme.
The question about possessing the Lord's treasures does not develop the punishment or misguidance claim.
Leaders are disowned by their followers when they see punishment and every bond between them is severed.
Followers wish to return so they can disown those they followed after seeing the punishment.
It forbids following the desires of people who went astray and led many others astray.
No soul bears another's burden, establishing a necessary boundary for the focus's account of added liability.
The earlier group tells the later group that each must taste punishment, completing the doubled-punishment exchange in 7:38.
Moses identifies Pharaoh and his chiefs as leading people astray from Allah's path and invokes judgment upon them.
Satan admits he only called people and they answered, denying coercion while leaving them accountable for their choice.
Satan has no authority over Allah's servants except those who follow him into error.
Hell is promised to all who follow Satan, giving the destination of that misguidance.
Misleaders bear their own burdens in full and burdens arising from those they lead astray without knowledge.
Each person is guided or astray for himself, and no bearer carries another's burden.
Satan and those who follow him are promised Hell as a full recompense.
Pharaoh leads his people astray and does not guide them, a concise leader-misguidance parallel.
Whoever takes Satan as an ally is led astray by him and guided toward the punishment of the Blaze.
Pharaoh and his leaders are made callers to the Fire and receive no help on the Day of Resurrection.
Disbelievers invite believers to follow their way and falsely offer to bear their sins.
Those misleaders bear their own burdens together with burdens arising from those they mislead.
Buying distracting speech to lead people from Allah's path is paired with humiliating punishment.
The condemned say they obeyed their leaders and great ones, who led them from the path.
They ask the Lord to give those leaders double punishment and a great curse.
Disbelievers argue before their Lord, beginning another judgment scene of mutual blame.
The arrogant leaders challenge the weak followers' claim that they prevented them from guidance.
Weak followers and arrogant leaders conceal regret when they see punishment, ending their mutual blame in a common judgment.
A burdened soul cannot carry another's burden, reinforcing the individual-accountability limit.
Humankind is warned not to worship Satan because he is a clear enemy.
Satan has already led a great multitude astray, directly naming wide-reaching misguidance.
The people addressed for that misguidance are told that this is the Hell they were promised.
The condemned turn on one another in questioning, opening a direct post-judgment blame exchange.
Followers accuse those before them of approaching them from the right side.
Those followed deny the charge by saying the others were not believers.
The leaders deny having authority over their followers, closely paralleling contested responsibility.
The word of punishment becomes binding upon both groups in the dispute.
The misleaders explicitly admit that they led the others astray because they themselves were astray.
Both groups share punishment on that Day, directly joining misguidance and common retribution.
The weak in the Fire ask the arrogant they followed whether they can remove any share of its punishment.
The arrogant answer that all are in the Fire and Allah has already judged between His servants.
Turning from the remembrance of the Most Merciful results in a devil assigned as a close companion.
Wrongdoers share in punishment on that Day, completing the companion-led misguidance sequence.
No bearer bears another's burden, another essential limit on reading added liability in the focus.
Satan tells a person to disbelieve, then disowns him once he disbelieves and punishment becomes imminent.
Both the deceiver and the deceived end in the Fire, remaining there as the recompense of wrongdoers.
Noah describes a people following those whose wealth and children only increase them in loss.
The leaders have led many astray, supplying a direct misguidance claim within Noah's appeal for judgment.
